The `camel-sanitizer` module is a checker for development and tests. It watches the calls of the steps of the routes
of a running Camel application and reports, when it happens, that a processor breaks the contract of `AsyncProcessor`:
-a callback called twice, or a processor that throws instead of calling its callback. It checks the code of Camel users
-as much as Camel's own: a custom `AsyncProcessor`, the producer of a custom component, a bean. A test that runs a
-broken path fails with a report that names the step and the class.
+a callback called twice, or a processor that throws instead of calling its callback. It also warns about a step whose
+callback has not come. It checks the code of Camel users as much as Camel's own: a custom `AsyncProcessor`, the
+producer of a custom component, a bean. A test that runs a broken path fails with a report that names the step and the
+class.
It checks the paths the tests run; it does not find untested ones.

+=== Still pending
+A call whose callback has not come is not a violation, as a slow endpoint looks the same, but it is what a hung
+exchange shows. When nothing happened in an exchange for `camel.sanitizer.pendingTimeout` (default `60s`: no call of a
+step, no return, throw or callback, also in its parts), the sanitizer logs a WARN with its innermost pending call: the
+step whose callback the exchange waits for, whether `process` returned, threw or has not returned yet (then with the
+stack of the thread that is still in it), and the enclosing calls that wait for it. The parts of an exchange are the
+correlated copies that a split, multicast, recipient list, enrich, kamelet, circuit breaker or a `to("kamelet:...")`
+step of it waits for: a copy that carries the id of the exchange as its correlation id while such a step is the
+innermost pending call of the exchange. Other copies, such as the one a `seda` producer queues, are exchanges of their
+own (unless the producing exchange is already in such a step when the copy starts). So a long split, or a
+`to("direct:...")` whose route is still busy, is not reported, and a step inside them that does not call back is. An
+exchange is not reported while it waits for its parts and they still have pending calls. Each call is reported once;
+if its callback comes later, an INFO line says after how long. A call that threw stays pending until its callback
+comes or the exchange is done (Camel catches the throw and fails the exchange; on older Camel versions the exchange
+hung there). The parts of a split with `shareUnitOfWork()` have no done event of their own: what they threw goes when
+their exchange is done. A call of a part that has not called back stays when its exchange is done, and is reported:
+the part may hang after the step that waited for it gave up, such as a split with a `timeout`. A recipient of a
+recipient list is not a step: a producer of a recipient that does not call back shows as the recipient list step still
+pending. Steps that wait on purpose for longer than the timeout are reported too: a delay or a throttle, a redelivery
+delay, a `pollEnrich` that waits, a processor that waits for something, or one that sends with a `ProducerTemplate` and
+waits for the reply. So are steps that wait for an exchange copy of their own, as the consumer side works on that copy,
+not on a part: a request-reply `to` over `seda` or `vm` whose consumer is slow but still making progress, and an
+`aggregate` step whose completion runs the aggregated exchange synchronously in the caller. A chaos `delay` on a step
+(a `step=` rule of camel-chaos), or at the entry of a route (a `route=` rule), runs before the step is called, so a
+delay longer than `pendingTimeout` shows up at the enclosing step that waits (such as a split, or the `to` of the
+calling route), and not at all at the top level of a route. A `delay` of an `endpoint=` or `component=` rule at a send
+(`at=send`) runs inside the send, so it shows at that `to` step. At a poll (`at=poll`) there is no exchange yet, so it
+is not seen; at the send of a dead letter channel (`at=dlq`) the error handler runs it after the failed step called
+back, so it shows like a `step=` delay.
+[source,text]
+Exchange sanitizer: callback still pending (R1, a warning)
+  exchange 5A1B...-0000000000000001, route route1, step lookup, processor com.acme.PriceLookup
+  called 60412 ms ago in CamelContext camel-1, and nothing happened in the exchange (its steps, and the steps of its parts) for 60012 ms
+  process returned false, and the callback has not been called
+  enclosing calls still pending: route route2 step to3

+  The callback of process(exchange, callback) must be called exactly once (see AsyncProcessor). This is a warning, not a violation: a slow endpoint looks the same (camel.sanitizer.pendingTimeout=60000 ms).
+The warnings never fail a test, and are not charged to it. When the context stops, the calls still pending then are
+listed at WARN (with `reportOnShutdown`), and the report on shutdown counts the warnings. The pending calls are kept in
+a table that holds ids and names, not the exchanges, with a bound of 10000 calls. The table is split in stripes, each
+with its own lock (twice the number of processors, rounded up to a power of two, at most 32), so routing threads that
+work on unrelated exchanges do not wait for each other; an exchange, its parts and the copies made from it while it is
+in the table are in one stripe. Each stripe has a share of the bound (10000 divided by the number of stripes), and the
+share is soft: a stripe past it drops its oldest calls only while all the stripes together hold more than 10000, so an
+asynchronous parallel split with many parts in flight is still watched. When calls are dropped, one WARN says that the
+checks are incomplete, and the report counts the calls dropped. The timeout is measured with `System.nanoTime()`, not
+with the time source of camel-test-dst, so a virtual clock does not stretch it.
+To know when an exchange is done, the sanitizer adds an event notifier of the exchanges completed and failed, so with
+the sanitizer on the exchange events of the context are fired (and the notifier is listed with the others, also in
+JMX). A pending timeout of `0` turns the warning off, and with it the table, the notifier and the list when the
+context stops.
+The parts of a split, multicast or recipient list are in the stripe of their exchange. With `parallelProcessing()`, the
+threads that run the parts therefore take the same lock of the table at each step call, return and callback. The lock is
+held briefly, but it costs more when the parts run on several threads, and it orders those threads, which can hide a
+race between parts that is not synchronized otherwise. To hunt races between the parts of a parallel split, set
+`camel.sanitizer.pendingTimeout=0`: the other checks of R1 stay on, and the table and its lock are not used.

+package org.apache.camel.sanitizer;
+import java.util.ArrayList;
+import java.util.Collection;

+ * The calls of steps whose callback has not come yet, per exchange, for the "still pending" warning of rule R1: a
+ * bounded map that keeps no exchange. It is keyed by the id of the exchange, so a part of a split, multicast or
+ * recipient list (or the copy that an enrich, kamelet, circuit breaker or {@code to("kamelet:...")} step works on)
+ * finds the exchange it belongs to by its correlation id, when the innermost pending call of that exchange is such a
+ * step; other correlated copies (such as the copy that a seda producer queues) are exchanges of their own, unless the
+ * producing exchange is already in such a step when the copy makes its first call (only a warning may then come later).
+ * It does not let an exchange that is gone take its entry with it (weak keys): a processor that drops the callback
+ * usually leaves nothing that refers to the exchange (the inflight repository keeps it only when browsing is on), so
+ * its entry would go exactly when the warning is needed.
+ * An exchange is reported when nothing happened in it for the timeout (no call of a step, return, throw or callback,
+ * also in its parts) and it does not wait for a part with a pending call: then only its innermost pending call, the one
+ * started last, is reported, once. So a split, or a {@code to("direct:...")}, that waits for steps that are still busy
+ * is not reported. A call that threw stays pending until its callback comes, or until the exchange is done: Camel
+ * catches the throw and fails the exchange, but before those fixes the exchange hung there. An exchange that is done
+ * (its unit of work, as the events of the exchange tell) is dropped, with the calls of its parts that threw. An
+ * exchange stays in the table while one of its parts has a pending call, also when its own calls have called back: the
+ * parts of a split with {@code shareUnitOfWork()} have no done event of their own, so the done event of the exchange
+ * drops what they threw. A call of a part that did not throw stays, as a call of an exchange of its own: the part may
+ * hang after the step that waited for it gave up (a timeout). An exchange whose parts have a pending call is not
+ * reported while it waits for them (its innermost call is the step that runs them).
+ * The table is split in stripes, each with its own lock, so that routing threads that work on unrelated exchanges do
+ * not wait for each other. An exchange stays in the stripe it is in; a new one goes to the stripe of the exchange it
+ * was copied from (its correlation id) when that exchange is in the table, else to the stripe its id hashes to. So an
+ * exchange, its parts, their parts and the other copies made while it is in the table are in one stripe (that of the
+ * outermost exchange), and each method for one exchange or call changes one stripe under its lock, as the single lock
+ * did before. Only the checker ({@link #stalled()}), the counts and the methods used when the context stops or a route
+ * is removed look at all the stripes, one at a time.
+ * The bound, {@link #MAX_PENDING} calls, is a safety net, not a sampling limit. Each stripe has a share of it
+ * ({@link #MAX_PENDING} divided by the number of stripes), and the share is soft: a stripe that holds more than its
+ * share sums the sizes of all the stripes without their locks, and drops its oldest calls (counted) only while they
+ * hold more than {@link #MAX_PENDING} in all. So one exchange and its parts, which are in one stripe, can hold nearly
+ * all of the bound, and a stripe within its share never looks at the others. The table then holds at most
+ * {@link #MAX_PENDING} plus the shares of the other stripes (less than twice the bound), give or take the calls made at
+ * the same moment in other stripes, as the sum is read without the locks. The ids of the parts (the {@code partOf} map,
+ * and the {@code partIds} of their exchange) are not counted in that bound: the id of a part goes when the part is
+ * done, or when its exchange leaves the table. The locks are held briefly and never while calling out.
+final class PendingCalls {
+     * The most pending calls kept, in all the stripes; a safety net, not a sampling limit.
+    static final int MAX_PENDING = 10_000;
+     * The most stripes.
+    static final int MAX_STRIPES = 32;
+    private final long timeoutNanos;
+    private final LongSupplier clock;
+    // whether a step (route id, step id) runs its work on correlated copies of the exchange and waits for them
+    private final BiPredicate<String, String> partStep;
+    private final Stripe[] stripes;
+    // the stripe of each exchange that has an entry in a stripe, or is a part there (its partOf); an entry is added and
+    // removed only under the lock of its stripe, and read without a lock to find that stripe
+    private final ConcurrentMap<String, Stripe> stripeOf = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
+    private final AtomicBoolean droppedOnce = new AtomicBoolean();
